items.title: Software Inventory Manager User Guide
items.text:
Software Inventory Manager (SIM) is a directory of the software that Jefferson Lab's Accelerator Controls Group (ACG) builds and maintains: apps, libraries, scripts and plugins, wherever their code lives. For each piece of software it records what it is, who maintains it and where to find it, and an assessment of its risk to operations that gives its Software Quality Assurance (SQA) control level. Software in GitHub, GitLab and the lab's other software lists is copied in by a sync; the rest is entered by hand.

At JLab, SIM is at ace.jlab.org/sim. Anyone can view it; log in to make changes, if you have an editor role.

The guide's website has a copy for each release; pick the version the Help tab shows. On GitHub, this guide describes the main branch, which may be newer than the version you are using.

items.title: Contents
items.text:
1. Concepts: software and its types, repositories, workflows, topics, maintainers, archived software, the risk assessment and roles.
  2. Directory: finding software, and adding, editing and removing it.
  3. Risk and SQA assessment: the six risk inputs, how to rate them, and how they give the SQA control level and the attention band.
  4. SQA elements: the checklist of what the SQAP asks of software at its control level, and finding the gaps.
  5. Repositories and sync: the Repositories tab, and copying software in from GitHub, GitLab and the lab's other lists.
  6. Administration: the Setup tab, settings and the sync's access tokens. For administrators.

items.title: Tabs at a glance
items.text: Tab What it is for Directory All the software, with filters; add, edit and assess it here. SIM opens on this tab. Repositories The places software lives, each with a link to its software and, if it can be synced, to its sync. Workflows The ways software is released, each with a link to its software and the SQA elements it provides. Setup Administrators only: settings and the directory cache. Help Version, contacts, documentation and a feedback form.

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
• Find software. On Directory, open the filter, give a name (* is a wildcard, as in *epics*), a maintainer's username, a topic or any of the other filters, and select Apply. Select a name to go to the software's home page. See Finding software.
  • Record software that isn't synced. On Directory, select Add, then give its name, type and repository, and anything else you know. See Adding software.
  • Assess its risk. Select the software's Risk & SQA cell, set the six inputs, and select Save. See Risk and SQA assessment.
  • Record what it has of the SQAP's elements. Once it is assessed, select SQA Elements in the same cell, set each element's status, and select Save. See SQA elements.
  • Bring in new software from GitHub or GitLab. On Repositories, select the arrow on the repository's row, check the differences, and apply them. See Repositories and sync.

items.title: Questions and changes
items.text: Use the feedback form on the Help tab, or contact the content and technical contacts listed there. To suggest a change to this guide, open an issue or pull request on GitHub.

items.title: Administration
items.text:
User Guide › Administration

This page is for SIM administrators: members of the sim-admin role, who see the Setup tab. Members of the acg role can edit software, assessments and syncs, but not the Setup tab; see Roles.

items.title: Setup tab
items.text: Page For Settings The app's settings; see Settings. Select a row, then Edit, to change its value. Directory Cache SIM caches users' names, emails and roles from Keycloak, and clears the cache every night at midnight. Clear it, or look up a user or role, after a change in Keycloak. Users must log out and in again for a change to their own roles to apply.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Setup › Settings lists the settings with their descriptions, by tag. Some changes can break the app or the Settings page itself, so that they can only be undone in the database. Changes made in the database directly take effect after Refresh Cache, at the top right of the page, or a redeploy; IP_READ_FILTER_ENABLED and IP_READ_URL_PATTERN always need a redeploy.

Setting Effect GITLAB_SYNC_EXCLUDE_CSV The GitLab groups and projects the GitLab sync leaves out; see below. SECRET_STORE_FILE_PATH The file with the syncs' access tokens; see Access tokens. NOTIFICATION_ENABLED, NOTIFICATION_MESSAGE, NOTIFICATION_LINK_NAME, NOTIFICATION_LINK_URL The banner at the top of every page. HELP_CONTENT_CONTACT, HELP_TECHNICAL_CONTACT The contacts on the Help tab. HELP_DOC_CSV The Help tab's documentation links: URL\|Label items separated by commas (neither can contain a comma). ADMIN_ROLE_NAME The role whose members the Help tab lists as admins, to logged-in users, and who get its feedback emails. It doesn't decide who sees the Setup tab, which is always the sim-admin role. EMAIL_ENABLED Turns on the Help tab's feedback emails, SIM's only email. EMAIL_TESTING_ENABLED Sends emails to the members of the testlead role instead, for testing. EMAIL_SENDER_ADDRESS The sender of feedback emails; the from address is the user's, from Keycloak. EMAIL_DOMAIN_NAME Unused: emails go to the addresses in Keycloak. IP_READ_FILTER_ENABLED, IP_READ_ALLOWLIST_PATTERN, IP_READ_URL_PATTERN Whether users outside the allowed addresses must log in to view pages. SMOOTHNESS_CDN_ENABLED, SMOOTHNESS_SERVER Where the pages' shared scripts and styles come from.

Server settings, such as the database connection and Keycloak, are environment variables and the application server's configuration; see the README.

items.title: Leaving GitLab projects out of the sync
items.text:
The GitLab sync reads every project in code.jlab.org's acc group and its subgroups, except those under the paths in GITLAB_SYNC_EXCLUDE_CSV. Each path is a group, which leaves out its subgroups and projects too, or a single project, such as acc/scratch or acc/ops/demo, as in the project's address on code.jlab.org. Paths are not case sensitive. To leave nothing out, set a path no project has, since a setting can't be empty.

Software already in SIM from a project you leave out shows as Remove on the next GitLab sync.

items.title: Access tokens
items.text:
The GitHub and GitLab syncs call those sites' APIs with access tokens, which SIM reads from a properties file, not the database:

GITHUB_ACCESS_TOKEN=... GITLAB_ACCESS_TOKEN=...

SECRET_STORE_FILE_PATH gives the file's path; a relative path is relative to the home directory of the user the application server runs as. SIM reads the file when it starts, so restart or redeploy it after changing the file or the setting. Without a token, its sync shows GITHUB_ACCESS_TOKEN is not set or GITLAB_ACCESS_TOKEN is not set; with one that has expired or lacks access, it shows Request failed with status code: 401.

The other three syncs read the lab's web pages without a token, so they work only where the application server can reach those pages.

items.title: Repositories, workflows and topics
items.text:
SIM has no page to add or change repositories, workflows or topics.

  • Repositories are rows in the database's REPOSITORY table: a name, description and home URL, and whether it can be synced (SYNC_YN). A repository can only be synced if SIM has code for it, which it has for the five named in What each sync reads; any other repository with SYNC_YN = 'Y' shows an Unknown Repository error on its sync.
  • The SQA elements a repository provides for all its software, which the Repositories tab lists and each product's checklist shows as met, are rows in the REPOSITORY_ELEMENT table: the repository, the element's id from SQA_ELEMENT, a note that says on what basis the repository provides it, and an optional link. Add a row only for an element that everything in the repository has. A change shows on the next page load.
  • Workflows are rows in the WORKFLOW table: a name, a description, and its place in the lists (WEIGHT). The syncs propose the workflows named Certified, CSUE, EPICS build system and Legacy Certified by those names, so one renamed in the database is proposed no more until SIM's code follows. To remove a workflow, first clear it from the software that has it (SOFTWARE.WORKFLOW_ID).
  • The SQA elements a workflow provides for all the software released with it, which the Workflows tab lists, are rows in the WORKFLOW_ELEMENT table, with the same columns as REPOSITORY_ELEMENT but for the workflow. Add a row only for an element that everything released with the workflow has; leave out one that some of it lacks, and it stays not recorded for each product. A change shows on the next page load.
  • Topics are added when someone types a new one in the Directory's dialog or a sync brings one in. A topic no software uses any more stays in the lists; remove it in the database.

items.title: Help tab
items.text: The Help tab shows the version, the contacts, the administrators (to logged-in users), the HELP_DOC_CSV links and a feedback form, which emails the members of the ADMIN_ROLE_NAME role. To link this guide from it, add an item such as https://jeffersonlab.github.io/sim/latest/|User Guide, the guide's website, or https://github.com/JeffersonLab/sim/blob/main/docs/user-guide/README.md|User Guide, its copy on GitHub, to HELP_DOC_CSV.

items.title: Concepts
items.text: User Guide › Concepts

items.title: Software
items.text:
Each entry in SIM is a piece of software, with:

Field What it is Name Its name, up to 128 characters. A name is unique within its repository; two repositories can each have software of the same name. Type APP, LIB (a library), SCRIPT or PLUGIN; see Types. Repository Where its code or release lives; see Repositories. Workflow How it is released, or none; see Workflows. Description What it does, up to 256 characters. Note Anything else worth knowing, up to 256 characters. A sync never changes it. Topics Tags such as java, epics or web; see Topics. Maintainers The usernames of the people who look after it, separated by commas. Home URL Its home page, such as its GitHub or GitLab project; the Directory links its name there. Archived Whether it is retired; see Archived software.

Each piece of software also has a risk assessment.

The name and repository identify the software: they can't be changed once it is added. To move software to another repository or rename it, add it again and remove the old entry.

items.title: Types
items.text:
Software is hard to sort into types, and a type is useful only if everyone sorts the same way, so take it as a best effort, decided by who the software is for and how it runs:

Type What it is APP Software for end users: a program with an entry point you run. Software started by a shared container to share resources, such as a web app, is an app too. SCRIPT A kind of app: small, narrowly focused, usually a single interpreted source file, run easily by power users. The line between an app and a script is blurry; when in doubt, choose APP. LIB Software for developers: code with no entry point of its own, meant to be reused by other software through its API. PLUGIN A kind of library that is added to or removed from an app easily, often by its users at run time, to customize it.

How ACG sorts common cases:

Software Type Why A Java web app in Wildfly, or PHP in Apache APP It is for end users. Strictly it is a plugin to its server, but it is used as an app. A desktop program started from JMenu APP It is for end users, and it is a program. A Low Level Apps IOC "glue" app APP It combines libraries into a program. A Java JAR that isn't executable, such as the jlog logbook API LIB It is for developers, to include in their code. Low Level Apps code that other software links LIB It is reusable code for developers.

Where one repository holds more than one kind of code, choose the type of its main purpose: an app with a container build file for a quick start is still an APP. A repository that holds only a container build file, or other infrastructure as code, is probably a SCRIPT.

items.title: Repositories
items.text:
A repository is a place software lives: a code host such as GitHub or GitLab, one of the lab's software lists, or a shared directory. The Repositories tab lists them.

Some repositories can be synced: SIM reads the list of software from the source and shows how it differs from SIM's, and an editor applies the differences. These are GitHub, GitLab, and the lab's Certified, CSUE and Low Level Apps lists; see What each sync reads. Software in other repositories is entered and kept up to date by hand. ACE_GIT and HLA_GIT, old local Git repositories, keep the few entries they have: add no new software to them.

The same software can be in more than one repository, because some lab lists record where software is deployed as well as where its code is kept: an app can be in CSUE for its deployment and on GitHub for its code and issues, such as fe_daq in CSUE and AI_SRF_OPS_fe_daq on GitHub. Each is a separate entry in SIM.

Administrators add repositories; see Repositories, workflows and topics.

items.title: Workflows
items.text:
A workflow is how software is released: how it is built, given a version and installed. Where software lives and how it is released are two things: a project on GitLab may be released with the certified workflow or without it. The Workflows tab lists them:

Workflow Is Certified The certified workflow on code.jlab.org: the release-workflow components, deployed to /cs/certified by ADM. GitHub web application Web applications on GitHub, released through GitHub Actions with the shared workflows. CSUE The Controls System UNIX Environment's release procedure. EPICS build system The EPICS build system, for low level apps. Legacy Certified The legacy Certified repository: tar-file releases, installed in versioned directories on NFS.

Software has one workflow, or none: none means nobody has said, not that it has no release procedure. An editor sets it in the Directory's edit dialog, and a sync proposes it for the software it adds where the repository tells: CSUE, Low Level Apps and the Certified list each release their software one way, and a GitLab project in the certified group uses the certified workflow. Other GitLab projects and GitHub repositories start with none.

Each row of the Workflows tab has the workflow's name, with a Software link that opens the Directory filtered to it, its description, and the SQA elements it provides for all the software released with it, each with its basis. The last row, None, links to the software whose workflow nobody has set.

Software that moves from the legacy Certified repository to code.jlab.org is added in GITLAB, with the Certified workflow; archive its old entry in CERTIFIED, which keeps Legacy Certified.

Administrators add workflows; see Repositories, workflows and topics.

items.title: Topics
items.text:
Topics are lower-case tags that group software across repositories, such as the language it is written in or the system it serves. A piece of software can have any number of topics, and the Directory's filter finds software that has all of the topics you pick.

GitHub and GitLab projects bring their own topics with them when synced. In the Directory's edit dialog you can pick existing topics or type a new one, up to 32 characters, which SIM then adds to the list.

For software synced from GitHub or GitLab, the topics app, lib, script and plugin also set its type when it is added; see Adding software from a sync.

items.title: Maintainers
items.text: Maintainers are usernames, such as jdoe, separated by commas. The Directory shows one per line, and its Maintainer Username filter finds software whose maintainers contain what you type, so jdoe finds jdoe alone or among others. SIM doesn't check that the usernames exist.

items.title: Archived software
items.text: Archived software is retired or no longer maintained, but kept for the record. The Directory leaves it out unless the Include Archived filter asks for it, and marks it with a 🕸 after its name. A sync from GitHub or GitLab sets it from the project's archived flag; for other software, an editor sets it.

items.title: Risk and SQA assessment
items.text:
Each piece of software has six risk inputs, each from 1 to 5: how much operations depend on it (Ops Impact), and five factors that make it harder to keep running: Code Complexity, Past Downtime Rate, Debug/Test Difficulty, Documentation Gaps and Esotericism. From them SIM works out:

  • the SQA control level, 0 Minimal to 3 Full, from Ops Impact and Code Complexity. This is the level of the Accelerator Controls Software Quality Assurance Plan (SQAP), which says how much process a change to the software needs. A documented exception can override it.
  • Fragility, the worst of the five factors.
  • Attention, Low, Moderate, High or Severe, from Ops Impact and Fragility: where improving documentation, testing or cross-training would most reduce the risk to operations.

Software starts Not assessed, with every input at its middle value, until someone saves an assessment. See Risk and SQA assessment.

items.title: SQA elements
items.text: The SQAP asks for certain SQA elements at each control level, such as a User Guide or version control. Assessed software has a checklist of the elements its level requires or recommends, each Met, a Gap, Not applicable or not recorded. An element that the software's workflow or repository provides for all its software, such as version control, is met without being recorded. See SQA elements.

items.title: Roles
items.text:
Who Can Anyone, logged in or not View the Directory, the Repositories and Workflows tabs, the sync pages, each assessment and checklist of SQA elements, and the Help tab. Members of the acg role Also add, edit and remove software, save assessments and checklists, and apply syncs. Members of the sim-admin role All of the above, and the Setup tab.

Roles come from the lab's identity provider (Keycloak). Log in with the link at the top right of any page. If a role was just given to you, log out and in again.

items.title: Directory
items.text:
User Guide › Directory

The Directory tab lists the software, ten to a page, and is where editors add, change and assess it. SIM opens on this tab.

items.title: The table
items.text:
Column Shows Name The name, linked to its home URL if it has one, with 🕸 if it is archived. Under it, the type and the repository, and the workflow if it has one. Description The description, then the note, then the topics. When there are five or more topics, the first three are shown and the rest are behind +N more; select it to show them all, and less to hide them again. Maintainers The maintainers' usernames, one per line. Risk & SQA The Ops Impact, the SQA level and the attention, or Not assessed. An asterisk after the SQA level means it is overridden; hover over it for the derived level and the rationale. Select the cell to open the assessment. Under it, for assessed software, SQA Elements: how many of the required SQA elements are met, and the gaps, or Not recorded. Select it to open the checklist.

The software is in order of risk: assessed software first, by Ops Impact from highest to lowest, then by attention from highest to lowest, then by name; then the software nobody has assessed yet, by name.

The line above the table says what the filter selects and how many match, such as All Software {1 - 10 of 245}. Select Previous and Next to page through, and Max Per Page to show 10 or 100 at a time.

items.title: Finding software
items.text:
Select Choose... at the top left of the page to open the filter, set what you want, and select Apply. The filters combine: software must match all of them. Clear empties the form; select Apply after it to see everything again.

Filter Finds Software Name Software with this name, ignoring case. Use * as a wildcard: epics* finds names that start with epics, and *epics* names that contain it. Maintainer Username Software whose maintainers contain this text, ignoring case. Repository Software in this repository. Workflow Software released with this workflow, or with None the software whose workflow nobody has set. Type Software of this type. Topics Software with all of the topics you pick. Include Archived Blank leaves archived software out, as it is by default; YES includes it, and EXCLUSIVELY shows only archived software. SQA Level Software at this SQA level: the override where there is one, else the derived level. Attention Software with this attention. Risk Factors Any factor ≥ 4: software with at least one of the five risk factors at 4 or 5, that is, a fragility of High or Fragile. Assessed Software that has been assessed, or that hasn't. Gap in SQA Element Software where this SQA element, or with Any element any of them, is recorded as a gap and is on the checklist at the software's level.

The SQA Level, Attention, Risk Factors and Gap in SQA Element filters only find assessed software, since SIM shows no level, attention or checklist for software nobody has assessed.

The filter is part of the page's address, so you can bookmark a search or send it to someone. The Software link beside each repository on the Repositories tab opens the Directory filtered to that repository, and the one beside each workflow on the Workflows tab opens it filtered to that workflow.

items.title: Editing software
items.text: Members of the acg and sim-admin roles see an Add button above the table. To edit or remove software, select its row, as the hint beside Add says.

items.title: Adding software
items.text:
Select Add, fill in the dialog, and select Save:

  • Name, Type and Repo (the repository) are required. A name already used in that repository is refused.
  • Workflow: how the software is released; see Workflows. Leave it at None if you don't know, or none of them fits.
  • Topics: pick from the list, or type a new topic and press Enter.
  • Maintainers: usernames separated by commas, such as jdoe,jsmith.
  • Archived: No for software in use.

New software starts not assessed. Software in a synced repository is usually added by its sync instead; software you add by hand to a synced repository shows as Remove on its next sync unless the source lists it too.

items.title: Editing
items.text:
Select the row's Name, Description or Maintainers cell to open the edit dialog. Links and buttons in those cells, such as the name's link to its home page and +N more, still do what they do, and dragging to select text in them doesn't open the dialog. The Risk & SQA cell opens the assessment instead. You can change everything but the name and the repository; to change either, add the software again and remove the old entry. Saving replaces the topics with the ones in the dialog.

Set the Workflow here when you know how the software is released: its checklist then shows the SQA elements the workflow provides as met.

A sync may later change what you edit: see What a sync changes. The note and the workflow are never synced, so the note is the place for anything you want kept.

items.title: Removing
items.text:
Archive retired software rather than removing it: it stays on record with its assessment, out of the Directory unless Include Archived asks for it; see Archived software. Remove is for software added by mistake, or the old entry of software you renamed or moved.

Open the row's edit dialog, select Remove at its bottom left, and confirm. The software, with its topics, its assessment and its SQA elements, is deleted; it can't be restored, only added again.

items.title: Embedding the Directory
items.text: /sim/directory?loose=Y shows the Directory on its own, without SIM's header and tabs, to embed in another page, such as a wiki, in a frame. It is always read-only, its software links open in the whole window rather than the frame, and it takes the same filters as the Directory: set them on the Directory, then add &loose=Y to its address. The risk assessments and the checklists of SQA elements still open, read-only.

items.title: Risk and SQA assessment
items.text:
User Guide › Risk and SQA assessment

Each piece of software has one assessment: six risk inputs, which give its Software Quality Assurance (SQA) control level and its attention band. Select the software's Risk & SQA cell in the Directory to open the Risk & SQA Assessment dialog. Anyone can open it to read; members of the acg and sim-admin roles can change it. Everyone else sees only Close.

The dialog has two links: SQAP §4.3, the Accelerator Controls Software Quality Assurance Plan's section on software control levels, and Guidance, which opens Rating the risk inputs in this guide.

items.title: Making an assessment
items.text:
1. Set the six Risk Inputs. As you change them, the dialog shows the derived SQA level, the fragility, the factors that set it, and the attention.
  2. If the SQAP allows an exception to the derived level, pick the level in Override and give the reason in Rationale, up to 512 characters. An override needs a rationale.
  3. Select Save. SIM saves the inputs, records you and the time as the assessor, and reloads the page. Cancel, the × in the title bar, or Esc closes the dialog without saving.

To drop an override, set Override to None and select Save; the rationale goes with it.

The footer of the dialog says who last assessed the software, and when.

items.title: Risk inputs
items.text:
Each input is from 1 to 5; the dialog shows each value's name and number.

Input 1 2 3 4 5 Used for Ops Impact Marginal Low Medium High Critical SQA level, attention Code Complexity Simple Low Medium High Complex SQA level, fragility Past Downtime Rate Rare Few Some Many Frequent Fragility Debug/Test Difficulty Easy Low Medium High Hard Fragility Documentation Gaps Few Low Medium High Many Fragility Esotericism Common Low Medium High Esoteric Fragility

Ops Impact is how much the accelerator's operation depends on the software. The other five are risk factors: what makes the software likely to fail, or slow to fix when it does.

items.title: Rating the risk inputs
items.text:
The risk that matters most is downtime: the software not working as operations need it, during a run or during Scheduled Accelerator Maintenance. Rate each input for the software as it is now, and reassess when the software or its use changes. Software not yet written, or a new version that a coming operations program needs, can be rated too.

The SQAP defines the two inputs that give the control level, so this guide doesn't repeat them. Its links go to the SQAP revision this release of SIM loads, a draft (0e98a07) whose text is on code.jlab.org; the SQAP's website has only released revisions.

  • Ops Impact: SQAP §4.3.1.
  • Code Complexity: SQAP §4.3.2.

Who rates the software, and when, is in SQAP §4.3.4. The other four inputs are SIM's own, and only set fragility and attention.

items.title: Past Downtime Rate
items.text: How often the software has failed in operations; past failures are the best guide to future ones. 1 Rare is software that has hardly ever failed, 5 Frequent software that fails often. The software's issues labeled downtime are the record to count.

items.title: Debug/Test Difficulty
items.text: How well tested the software is, and how hard it is to test and debug. Consider whether it has unit and integration tests and a log; whether its code is modular, so that a problem can be isolated; whether it is easy to trace what it is doing; and whether debugging needs special tools or beam studies. Software that has run in production for a long time can count as tested in place; new, untested software rates higher. 1 Easy is well tested and easy to debug, 5 Hard is poorly tested or hard to debug.

items.title: Documentation Gaps
items.text: What documentation the software is missing: a README, API documentation (such as Javadoc, Doxygen or Sphinx), a user guide, on-call notes, technical notes such as a design or administration guide, and requirements. Poorly defined requirements are a risk of their own: software that doesn't do what operations need is downtime too. 1 Few is comprehensive documentation, 5 Many is sparse. The aim is that no knowledge lives only in someone's head.

items.title: Esotericism
items.text: How much specialized knowledge the software hides, beyond what its documentation can pass on: its subject domain, its programming language and libraries, its development environment and tools, and its procedures and customers. The fewer people in ACG who understand it well enough to troubleshoot it, the higher the rating; it is relative to ACG's staff, not to the world. 1 Common is widely understood, 5 Esoteric is software only one person knows. The aim is at least two experts, a primary maintainer and a backup, and a few others familiar with its technology and subject.

items.title: SQA control level
items.text:
The SQA control level says how much process the SQAP asks for when the software changes: 0 Minimal, 1 Partial, 2 Significant or 3 Full. SIM derives it from Ops Impact and Code Complexity with the SQAP's control level table, and the dialog shows the result as you change them.

An override replaces the derived level with another, for an exception the SQAP allows. The Directory then shows the override with an asterisk, and its SQA Level filter uses the override. The derived level is kept, so the dialog shows both.

items.title: Fragility and attention
items.text:
Fragility is the worst of the five risk factors, from 1 Robust to 5 Fragile; the dialog names the factors that set it. A single bad factor makes software fragile, however good the others are.

Attention says where effort would most reduce the risk to operations. SIM derives it from Ops Impact and fragility:

Ops Impact \ Fragility 1 Robust 2 Low 3 Medium 4 High 5 Fragile 1 Marginal Low Low Low Moderate Moderate 2 Low Low Low Moderate Moderate High 3 Medium Low Moderate Moderate High High 4 High Moderate Moderate High High Severe 5 Critical Moderate High High Severe Severe

Unlike the SQA level, attention is meant to fall as the software improves: documenting it, adding tests or training a second maintainer lowers a factor, and with it the fragility and the attention. Reassess the software when that happens. To choose what to work on next, filter the Directory by attention, or by Risk Factors for software with any factor at 4 or worse.

items.title: Not assessed
items.text: New software has every input at 3, or Some for Past Downtime Rate, and shows Not assessed until someone selects Save in its dialog, even if they keep those values. Not-assessed software comes last in the Directory, and the SQA Level, Attention and Risk Factors filters leave it out. To find the software still to be assessed, set the Directory's Assessed filter to Not assessed.

items.title: SQA elements
items.text:
User Guide › SQA elements

The Accelerator Controls Software Quality Assurance Plan (SQAP) asks different things of software at each SQA control level: a User Guide at Significant and Full, version control at Partial and above, and so on. SIM keeps a checklist of these SQA elements for each piece of software, so that you can see which of them it has, and find the software that lacks one.

The checklist follows the control level, so only assessed software has one. Select SQA Elements in the software's Risk & SQA cell in the Directory to open the SQA Elements dialog. Anyone can open it to read; members of the acg and sim-admin roles can change it. Everyone else sees only Close.

items.title: What is on the checklist
items.text:
The dialog lists the elements the SQAP asks for at the software's control level, the override where there is one: first those it requires, under a Required heading, then those it recommends, under Recommended, each in the SQAP's order. Each heading counts its elements, and so does the line above the table, so a change of level shows in the numbers.

Each element has the SQAP's short label, such as Dependency choices recorded; hover over it for the SQAP's full wording, such as "Choice recorded: purpose, source, license, maintenance status". Under the label are the element's phase and a link to the section of the SQAP that describes it, in the revision SIM loaded the elements from. While that is a draft, the link opens the SQAP's source on code.jlab.org at that revision: the SQAP's website publishes only released revisions, and the latest of those may not have the draft's elements.

The checklist holds the elements a product has or lacks as a whole, such as a Software Requirements Specification, a User Guide, version control and issue tracking. What the SQAP asks of each change, such as a code review or a deployment plan, is recorded in the change's merge request and in ATLis, not here.

The elements and the levels that require them come from the SQAP itself, which publishes them as data with each revision. The line under the table names the revision SIM has.

When the control level changes, the checklist changes with it. What was recorded of an element the new level doesn't ask for is kept, and comes back if the level does.

items.title: Met, by the workflow or the repository
items.text:
Some elements come with how the software is released or where it lives, not with the software: the certified workflow installs each release in a folder for its version, and every project on GitLab is under version control and has an issue tracker. Such an element is kept once, for the workflow or the repository, and is met for all its software without anyone recording it. The Workflows and Repositories tabs list what each provides.

In the dialog, the status of such an element reads Met, by and what provides it, such as Met, by the Certified workflow or Met, by GITLAB, where another reads Not recorded, with the basis under it. An element's status is, in order: what was recorded for the software; otherwise met by its workflow or its repository; otherwise not recorded. Where both provide an element, the dialog names the workflow.

A status recorded for the software replaces the provider's. If a project has its issue tracker switched off, record a Gap; the dialog then says Otherwise met by the provider. To go back to the provider's, set the status to Met, by the provider again.

Met, by a workflow or a repository means it provides the element for all its software, on the basis shown. Nobody has looked at this software's.

What a workflow doesn't provide is not a gap. CSUE and the EPICS build system install software under developers' usernames, so they don't provide Read-only install (installed software read-only to its users): for software released with them the element stays Not recorded until somebody records it.

Software gets what its workflow provides only once it has one: set it in the Directory's edit dialog, unless its sync did.

To keep a link or a note on such an element, type it: the status changes to Met, recorded for the software, with the provider as Otherwise met by.

items.title: Set by SIM
items.text:
SIM sets two elements itself, from what it already records, and nobody records them:

  • Ratings recorded (Ops Impact and Code Complexity recorded in the Software Directory) is met by the assessment, which every checklist comes from. The dialog names who assessed the software, and when.
  • Two maintainers (at least two maintainers listed in the Software Directory) is met when the Directory's Maintainers lists two or more, and a gap when it lists fewer. Add a maintainer in the edit dialog to meet it.

Their status reads Set by SIM and can't be changed in the dialog. They count like any other element, and the Gap in SQA Element filter finds software with fewer than two maintainers where its level asks for two.

items.title: Recording an element
items.text:
For each element, set:

Field Means Status Met: the software has the element. Gap: it should have it, and doesn't. Not applicable: the element doesn't apply to this software. Not recorded: nobody has said. Link For an element that is met, where it is: the line under the link says what the SQAP expects there, such as "The lock file; where the build tool has none, the build file or README that gives exact versions". For a gap, the issue that tracks it. A web address that starts with http:// or https://, up to 512 characters. Optional. Note Anything else, up to 512 characters. Not applicable needs a note that says why.

Then select Save. SIM saves the checklist and reloads the page. Cancel, the × in the title bar, or Esc closes the dialog without saving. A link or a note needs a status: to clear an element, set it to Not recorded, or to Met, by its workflow or repository, and empty its link and note.

Under each status is who last recorded the element, and when. Saving the checklist doesn't change that for the elements you left as they were.

Once an element has a link, Open beside it opens the link in a new window, for anyone reading the checklist, logged in or not.

The line under each link comes from the SQAP with the elements, and says where to look, not what the element must contain: follow the element's section link for that. Several elements can have the same link, as the four about dependencies do when one section of the README covers them. The two elements SIM sets have no link, and no line.

Met means somebody says the software has the element, not that the element is good enough: SIM doesn't read the document behind the link.

items.title: Not recorded is not a gap
items.text:
The SQAP brings existing software under the plan at its next planned change, and asks for nothing to be written before then for its own sake. So an empty checklist is not a finding: the Directory shows Not recorded, as it shows Not assessed for software nobody has rated, and counts no gaps. Record a Gap when the software has come under the plan and lacks the element.

What a workflow or a repository provides doesn't change this: software whose checklist nobody has touched shows Not recorded, though the dialog shows the elements they provide as met.

items.title: In the Directory
items.text:
The Risk & SQA cell shows, under the assessment, how many of the required elements are met, such as 5 of 7, and the number of gaps if there are any:

  • The second number is the required elements that apply: those recorded as Not applicable are left out.
  • Recommended elements are outside both numbers. A gap in one still counts as a gap.
  • An element met by the workflow or the repository counts as met.
  • Not recorded means nobody has recorded any element of the checklist.

To find software with a gap, set the Directory's Gap in SQA Element filter to an element, or to Any element. It finds software where the element is recorded as a gap and is on the checklist at the software's level.

items.title: Documentation Gaps
items.text: The assessment's Documentation Gaps input is still a rating that a person sets. The checklist doesn't set it or change the fragility; use the checklist's gaps to judge it.

items.title: Repositories and sync
items.text: User Guide › Repositories and sync

items.title: The Repositories tab
items.text:
The Repositories tab lists the places software lives. Each row has:

  • the repository's name, linked to its home page if it has one, and a Software link that opens the Directory filtered to the repository;
  • its description;
  • the SQA elements it provides for all its software, each with its basis: these are met on the checklist of every product in the repository, unless a status is recorded for the product;
  • a Sync arrow (→), which opens the repository's sync. The arrow is disabled for repositories that can't be synced, whose software is entered by hand.

items.title: What a sync does
items.text:
A sync reads the list of software from the repository's source, compares it with the software SIM has in that repository, archived software included, and lists the differences for an editor to apply. Nothing changes in SIM until someone applies them.

Opening the sync page reads the source again, so it shows the source as it is now, and a large source takes a while to load. If SIM can't read the source, the page shows an error instead of the table.

Software is matched by name, within the repository. The line above the table counts the records read from the source and those in SIM, and how many are matched, to add, to remove and to update. The rows come in that order:

Row Means Button Green In the source but not in SIM. Add Remote value (green) above SIM's (red) In both, but the source has changed. Update Red In SIM but no longer in the source. Remove Plain In both, and the same. None

Members of the acg and sim-admin roles can apply each row with its button, or all of them at once with Apply All, which first asks you to confirm how many it will update, remove and add. Each applied row shows Success!, and Apply All shows Done! when it has finished. Open the sync again to check that nothing is left.

Anyone else sees the same page, with the buttons disabled.

Check the Remove rows before applying them. Remove deletes the software from SIM, with its note, its risk assessment and its SQA elements, and can't be undone. A project that was renamed shows as one Remove and one Add, and applying both loses the old entry's assessment, SQA elements and note: add them to the new entry before removing the old one. A project that left the source, such as a GitHub repository that lost its acg topic, shows as Remove, and so does software added to a synced repository by hand.

items.title: Adding software
items.text:
Added software gets the name, description, topics, home URL and archived flag the source gives, and maintainers from the sources that list them (CSUE and Low Level Apps). Its type is:

  • for GitHub and GitLab, from its topics: app, lib, script or plugin, the first of these it has in that order, or APP if it has none of them;
  • for the Certified list, the section it is listed in (apps, libraries or scripts);
  • for CSUE and Low Level Apps, APP.

Its workflow is the one the sync proposes, shown in the row's Workflow column, where the repository tells how its software is released:

  • for CSUE, CSUE; for Low Level Apps, EPICS build system; for the Certified list, Legacy Certified;
  • for GitLab, Certified for a project in the certified group, acc/ops/acs/certified or a subgroup of it, and none for any other;
  • for GitHub, none.

Set or correct it afterwards in the Directory's edit dialog.

Like any new software, it starts not assessed.

items.title: Updating software
items.text:
A sync compares, and Update copies from the source:

  • the description, when the source has one;
  • the topics, when the source has any;
  • the home URL, when the source has one;
  • the archived flag, from GitHub and GitLab only.

It never changes the type, the workflow, the maintainers, the note or the assessment, so edits to those in SIM are kept: the Workflow column of software SIM already has shows its own, whatever the sync would propose. A GitLab project that moves into the certified group keeps the workflow it has until an editor changes it. An edit to a field the source does have, such as a description, shows as Update on the next sync, and applying it puts the source's value back: change those at the source instead.

items.title: What each sync reads
items.text:
Repository Reads Gives GITHUB The JeffersonLab organization's GitHub repositories with the topic acg. Name, description, topics, home URL, archived. GITLAB The projects in the acc group on code.jlab.org, with its subgroups, except the groups and projects an administrator leaves out. Name, description, topics, home URL, archived. CERTIFIED The Certified Software list's apps, libraries and scripts. Name, description, home URL. CSUE The Controls System UNIX Environment apps page. Name, description, maintainer (the directory owner), home URL. LLAPP The Low Level Apps listing. Name and maintainer (the file owner) only.

Topics are made lower case. To bring a GitHub repository into SIM, give it the acg topic; to take a GitLab project out, an administrator adds its path to the sync's exclusions.
